# War games and operations research (`wargaming_operations_research`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by probability_statistics, general_staff_war_college, map_projection_charts, game_theory
- Core idea: Two methods to test decisions without paying in lives. In a war game two teams move units on a true map under an umpire who uses tables from real experience and dice for chance, so plans meet a thinking opponent and time and space are honest. Operations research treats operations as an experiment: count what actually happened and work out the best use of what you have. Example: British analysts found in 1942–1943 that convoy losses depended on the number of attackers and escorts and hardly on convoy size, so fewer, larger convoys lost a smaller share of ships.
- Pitfalls:
  - Umpires who let the home side win; the Japanese re-floated their sunk carriers in the war game before Midway
  - Survivorship bias: armour belongs where the returning bombers show no holes (Wald), because those hit there did not come back
  - Measuring what is easy to count instead of what decides the outcome
  - A model is only as good as the data from real operations fed into it
- History: india: c. 6th c. AD – chaturanga, a board game of the four arms of an army, ancestor of chess; china: ancient – weiqi (go) used as a metaphor and training of strategic thought; europe: 1824 – Reisswitz's Kriegsspiel adopted by the Prussian army; 1916 – Lanchester's equations of combat; 1940–1943 – Blackett's groups apply operational research to radar, anti-submarine war and convoys; americas: 1942 – US Navy anti-submarine operations research group (Morse); 1943 – Abraham Wald's survivability studies
- Read:
  - Philip M. Morse & George E. Kimball, Methods of Operations Research (1951)
  - Stephen Budiansky, Blackett's War (2013)
  - Peter P. Perla, The Art of Wargaming (1990)
